## TL;DR

Fixed the review finding where the periodic validation-container reaper could treat age alone as proof that a container was abandoned. The reaper now runs only when the host reports no effective slot occupancy, temporarily blocks new local dispatch while it inspects and removes candidates, and filters/rechecks names owned by active runs. This matters because the 25-minute execution limit can be preceded by as much as 15 minutes of host-lock waiting. The changed-path check passed on the current branch tree.

## Work and rationale

The review identified a concrete mismatch between the reaper's age threshold and the maximum time a legitimate run can remain active. The previous implementation listed prefixed containers and removed any created more than 25 minutes ago. However, the remote command can include the full lock-wait allowance before the validation starts. A container that belongs to a healthy run could therefore cross the reaper threshold while the run is still active.

I changed the host pool's reaper scheduling so it starts only when `effectiveActive` is zero. That value includes both the server's active slots and observed host-side lock occupancy. Once scheduled, the host enters a short reaping state; dispatch treats that state as unavailable until the remote listing/removal attempt settles. This closes the local race where a new pool run could start between the idle check and the cleanup round-trip.

Candidate selection also accepts the set of active container names. The reaper excludes those names from the stale list and checks ownership again immediately before requesting removal. The second check covers an ownership change between listing and iterating candidates. These name checks are defense in depth alongside the no-active-slot gate.

The test fixture now includes an old, prefixed candidate that is explicitly marked active and confirms that it is not selected, while the abandoned old candidate remains eligible. Documentation now explains the lock-wait allowance and the reaper's idle/dispatch guard instead of claiming age alone makes active ownership impossible.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted the task's RepoOS-managed sync before editing, because the live landability report had identified a conflict in `src/ui-app/src/stores/repo.ts`. RepoOS refused the sync with `Task #1049 has an agent turn in progress`. After the changed-path check finished, I retried; RepoOS returned the same refusal. I did not bypass the RepoOS ownership guard or manipulate the main checkout. The implementation and check were completed in the assigned worktree.

For the reaper, I considered raising its age threshold to cover the combined timeout. That would leave a window where a container is retained based on a guessed maximum duration and could delay cleanup of genuinely leaked containers. The ownership-aware idle gate better captures the condition the code needs: whether a run can currently own a container on that host.

## Challenges and blockers

The code and documentation changes passed the requested `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. Remote validation passed on ThinkPad. The check ran 274 scoped test files (3,799 passed, 1 skipped), the second boot-timing pass (2 passed), formatting, lint, build, UI smoke, rendered contrast, and the remaining selected safety checks; all reported success.

The outstanding blocker is the RepoOS sync guard. The task's live landability result had also reported a merge conflict with current `main` in `src/ui-app/src/stores/repo.ts`. Since `repoos sync 1049` continues to refuse while the engineer turn is active, this draft does not claim that the conflict was resolved or that the branch is landable. The sync and a post-sync check still need to run once RepoOS permits them.

## Key learnings

Container age is not a reliable proxy for ownership when queue/lock time is charged separately from the nominal run cap. The reaper must coordinate with the same host activity signals used for dispatch, and dispatch needs to remain paused while cleanup is in flight. The review also exposed a documentation risk: statements that a container “cannot” be active after a duration need to account for all timeout components, including lock acquisition.
